To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of different renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) blockers in patients with diabetes mellitus showed similar effects on major cardiovascular and kidney outcomes, and the use of combination of RAAS blockers did not improve the outcomes.

, in adult patients with diabetes, there is a lack of evidence to support that any of the three classes of RAS inhibitors is superior to others with respect to the risk of cardiovascular and renal complications, with the exception of a possible advantage of ACE inhibitors over ARBs in the prevention of stroke and of ACE inhibitor plus ARBs over ACE inhibitor monotherapy in the prevention of angina.

, in adults with diabetes, compared with ACE inhibitor monotherapy, no other RASS blocker used in monotherapies and/or combination was significantly more effective on major cardiovascular or renal outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of the effects of the renin– angiotensin system blockers in the treatment of diabetes mellitus.
the use of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors in the treatment of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
the use of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) blockers in patients with diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in adults with diabetes, the effects of ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and DR inhibitors are similar on major cardiovascular and kidney outcomes.
the RAS blockers are all effective in preventing major cardiovascular events in patients with diabetes.
ACE inhibitor monotherapy and ARBs are equally effective in reducing major cardiovascular and renal complications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of RAS blockers for preventing cardiovascular and kidney complications in patients with type 2 diabetes is not associated with significant differences in clinical effectiveness among the different classes.
the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is a complex system that regulates the blood pressure and the fluid and electrolyte homeostasis.
the renin–Angiotension system (RAS), which is a hormone system that controls blood pressure and fluid balance, has been a target for drug development for decades.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are no differences in the effects of ACE inhibitors versus ARBs on the main cardiovascular and renal outcomes of diabetes.
there is no difference between ACE inhibitors and angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs) in preventing cardiovascular events in patients with diabetes.
there are no differences in the effectiveness of the different classes of RAS blockade in the prevention of cardiovascular and renal complications.
